Calculate DEAR\n\n   • Step 1: Calculate Modified Duration (MD)\n    MD = D/(1+R) = 6/1.075 = 5.581\n\n   • Step 2: Calculate price volatility\n       Price volatility = 5.581 * 1.65 * 0.0022 = 0.02026\n\n   • Step 3: Calculate DEAR\n    DEAR = Market value of position * Price volatility = 1,000,000*0.02026 = $20,260\n\n     The potential daily loss in earnings on the $1 million position is $20,260 if the 1 bad day in 100 occurs tomorrow.\n             √        √\n       b. Liquidity risk arises for two reasons:\n  • Liability side\n       • When an FI’s liability holders, such as depositors or insurance policyholders, seek to cash in\n            their financial claims immediately.\n  • Asset side\n       • The exercise of loan commitments and other credit lines by borrowers.\n       • Change of the value of investment securities portfolios due to unexpected changes of interest\n            rates.\n  • Consequence: the DI has to (i) borrow additional funds or (ii) sell assets.\n\n\n\n\n\n                                                                                                                       33 / 84","w":699,"h":393},{"i":"","t":"Liquidity risk\n\n\n - Liquidity can be managed by two approaches:\n\n\n    Purchased liquidity management                         - Stored liquidity management\n\n      - Liquidity can be purchased in financial markets,    - Liquidate assets.\n     e.g.  borrowed funds from competitor banks and    - Decreases size of balance sheet.\n     other institutional investors.                                - Requires holding excess non-interest bearing as-\n      - Managing the liability side preserves asset side of   sets (hold excess low-rate assets in the form of cash\n    balance sheet.                                on its balance sheet).\n      - Borrowed funds are likely to be at higher rates\n    than interest paid on deposits, that is funds to be\n    borrowed at market rates.\n      - Purchased liquidity management allows DIs to\n    maintain their overall balance sheet size.\n\n\n\n\n\n                                                                                                                       34 / 84","w":699,"h":393},{"i":"","t":"Liquidity risk\n\n\n\nFinancing Gap\n\n                    Financing Gap = Average Loans −Average Deposits\n\n - If Financing Gap > 0, the DI must fund it by using its cash and liquid assets and/or\nborrowing funds in the money market. Thus:\n\n                    Financing Gap = −Liquid Assets + Borrowed Funds\n\n or\n         Financing Gap + Liquid Assets = Financing Requirement (Borrowed Funds)\n\n\n\n\n\n                                                                                                                       35 / 84","w":699,"h":393},{"i":"","t":"Liquidity risk\n\n\n Liquidity index\n - Liquidity index measures the potential losses an FI could suffer from a sudden or fire-sale disposal of\n assets compared with the amount it would receive at a fair market value established under normal\n market (sale) conditions.\n\n\n                                       N\n                                                                 I = X wi(Pi/P∗i )\n                                                 i=1\n\n where:\nPNi=1 wi = 1\n Pi: The immediate fire-sale asset price.\nP∗i : The fair market price.\n Note: The greater the differences between immediate fire-sale asset prices and fair market prices, the\n less liquid is the DI’s portfolio of assets.\nThe smaller the liquidity index, the higher liquidity risk the DI faces.\n\n\n\n\n                                                                                                                       36 / 84","w":699,"h":393},{"i":"","t":"Liquidity risk\n\n\n\n\n Example: Bank X has two assets: 50% in one-month Treasury bills and 50% in real estate loans.\n - If the DI must liquidate its T-bills today (P1), it receives $99 per $100 of face value.  If it can wait to\n liquidate them on maturity (in one month’s time), it will receive $100 per $100 of face value (P∗1 ).\n - If the DI has to liquidate its real estate loans today, it receives $85 per $100 of face value (P2).\n Liquidation at the end of one month (closer to maturity) will produce $92 per $100 of face value (P∗2 ).\n\n      Calculate the liquidity index.\n\n\n                            N\n                                            I = X wi(Pi/P∗i ) = 0.5 ∗99 + 0.5 ∗85 = 0.957                                               100       92\n                                   i=1\n\n\n\n\n\n                                                                                                                       37 / 84","w":699,"h":393},{"i":"","t":"What is next?\n\n\n1. An account holder has maintained an average balance of $500 for the first six months and\n $1,000 for the remaining six months. The account holder writes an average of 60 cheques per month\nand pays $0.02 per cheque, although it costs the bank $0.05 to clear a cheque.\n\n     What average return does the account holder earn on the cheque account?\n\n      Gross interest return = Explicit interest return + Implicit interest return\n\n       Explicit interest = Interest earned by account holder = ($500*0.00*6/12) + ($1,000*0.04*6/12) = $20\n\n       Implicit interest = Fee earned on cheques = ($0.05 - $0.02)*60*12 = $21.60\n\n      Gross interest return: $20 + $21.6 = $41.6\n\n      Average interest earned = $41.60/$750 = 5.55%\n\n\n\n\n\n                                                                                                                       40 / 84","w":699,"h":393},{"i":"","t":"Liability and Liquidity management\n\n\n\n\nA cheque account requires a minimum balance of $750 for interest to be earned at an annual rate of 4\n per cent. The account holder writes an average of 60 cheques per month\nand pays $0.02 per cheque, although it costs the bank $0.05 to clear a cheque.\n\n     What is the average return if the bank lowers the minimum balance to $400?\n\n       Explicit interest = Interest earned by account holder = ($500*0.04*6/12) + ($1,000*0.04*6/12) = $30\n\n       Implicit interest = Fee earned on cheques = ($0.05-$0.02)*60*12 = $21.60\n\n      Gross interest return: $30 + $21.6 = $51.6\n\n      Average interest earned = $51.60/$750 = 6.9%\n\n\n\n\n\n                                                                                                                       41 / 84","w":699,"h":393},{"i":"","t":"Liability and Liquidity management\n\n\n\n\nA cheque account requires a minimum balance of $750 for interest to be earned at an annual rate of 4\n per cent. The two-step procedure for contingent guaranty contracts (non-market-related OBS\n transactions: Loan commitments, standby L/C,...)\n   • Step 1: The notional amount of the transaction must be converted into an on-balance-sheet equivalent,\n       called a credit equivalent amount (CEA).\n    CEA is determined by multiplying the notional amount by a credit conversion factor (CCF).\n   • Step 2: CEA must be multiplied by the appropriate risk weight (the risk weights are the same as those\n      used for on-balance-sheet assets).\n\n\n\n\n\n                                                                                                                       47 / 84","w":699,"h":393},{"i":"","t":"Calculate capital ratio\n\n\nExample: Step 1\n\n\n        OBS item                   Face value ($m)   Conversion factor   Credit equivalent amount\n\n           Two-year loan commitment    80            50%            80*50% = 40\n           Standby letter of credit       10            100%            10*100% = 10\n             Trade-related letter of credit   50            20%            50*20% = 10\n\nStep 2:\n\n\n   OBS item                             Credit equivalent amount   Risk weight   Risk-weighted asset equivalent\n\n    Two-year loan commitment (B+)     40                   150%       40*150% = 60\n    Standby letter of credit (BBB)       10                   100%       10*100% = 10\n     Trade-related letter of credit (BBB)   10                   100%       10*100% = 10\n     Total                                                                 80\n\n\n\n\n\n                                                                                                                       48 / 84","w":699,"h":393}]
